analysis|01-18|1974|Συμφωνία αποδέσμευσης Ισραήλ και Αιγύπτου|Israel and Egypt sign a disengagement agreement|After the Yom Kippur War of 1973, Israel and Egypt found themselves in a military deadlock. The United States took on a mediating role, with Henry Kissinger making repeated visits to the region. The diplomacy of the era aimed at containing the conflict. The agreement included two successive phases, with the second following a few years later. // On 18 January 1974 the agreement on the disengagement of forces in the Suez area was signed, which provided for the withdrawal of troops to defined zones. The agreement also included control zones with the presence of United Nations forces. Although limited, it opened the way to further agreements. Kissinger travelled many times between the capitals of the region to keep the negotiations on course. // The agreement was the first step in a long process that led to the Camp David accords and to the peace of 1979. The stabilisation of the Suez area played an important role in relations between Egypt and Israel. This diplomatic process remains an example for international negotiations. The agreement became a model for other efforts to settle conflicts in the Middle East. Understanding the context of the era helps in interpreting the decisions taken then. The discussion on the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life.

analysis|01-19|1853|Πρεμιέρα του «Τροβατόρε»|Premiere of Il Trovatore|In the mid-nineteenth century Italian opera flourished greatly, with Giuseppe Verdi at the forefront. Composers sought subjects with intense drama, passion and political reference. The audiences of the era were passionate about melodies and vocal performances. The premiere coincided with a time when Italian operas were often discussed for their political dimension. // On 19 January 1853 the opera "Il Trovatore" was presented for the first time in Rome, at the Teatro Apollo. The work, based on a Spanish play, recounted a complex plot of revenge and romantic conflicts. Its music included particularly well-known arias and demanding vocal lines. The music of the work is characterised by intensely dramatic passages and by lyrical melodies that alternate. // The opera soon became widely known in Europe and the world, and it remains one of the most performed works in the repertoire. Its success strengthened Verdi's reputation as the leading composer of the era. The work continues to move audiences with its dramatic power. The story of Il Trovatore is still presented around the world and is associated with the name of Verdi. The discussion on the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life.

analysis|01-19|1960|Σύμφωνο ασφάλειας ΗΠΑ και Ιαπωνίας|US-Japan security treaty is signed|After the Second World War, Japan was under the military presence of the United States, with the agreement of 1951 regulating the bases and security. This cooperation provoked reactions in Japanese society, which demanded greater autonomy. The relations of the two countries were deeply influenced by the Cold War and by Asian balances. The treaty was ratified after extensive debates in the Japanese Diet. // On 19 January 1960 the two countries signed the Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security in Washington. The agreement stipulated that each party would treat an attack on the territory of the other as a common threat. At the same time, it regulated the presence of American forces on Japanese soil. The signing provoked large demonstrations in Tokyo. The protests against the treaty were among the most intense of the post-war period. // The treaty remains the basic framework of American-Japanese cooperation to this day. The security of the Pacific region became a key issue for the two countries. The reactions of that era influenced later Japanese policy. The agreement thus constitutes one of the most important points of Asian international relations. The treaty has been a central pillar of Japan's foreign policy for decades. This historical development continues to be studied by researchers and historians around the world.

analysis|01-19|1983|Η Apple παρουσιάζει το Lisa|Apple unveils the Lisa|In the early 1980s personal computers were used mainly for text and command lines. The idea of a graphical environment with a mouse had been developed in research centres, such as Xerox PARC. Apple sought to bring this technology to the market. Its design was very complex and required powerful hardware, which raised the cost of production. // The Lisa was presented in January 1983 and was the first personal computer with a graphical environment and mouse to be sold on a large scale. Its price was high, so its commercial spread was limited compared with expectations. The device had innovative features for the era, such as windows and icons. Apple faced difficulties in marketing the product and in competing with cheaper computers. // The Lisa paved the way for the Macintosh, which was presented shortly afterwards and enjoyed much greater success. The experience showed how important the relation between price and usability is. Today graphical environments with a mouse are the dominant form of computer use. The innovation of the Lisa is regarded as a turning point for the design of personal computing. This experience helped the company adjust its strategy for its later products.

analysis|01-20|1921|Το πρώτο Σύνταγμα της Τουρκίας|Turkey's first constitution|After the First World War the Ottoman Empire had collapsed and a large part of Anatolia was under foreign occupation. Mustafa Kemal organised a national resistance in Ankara, with the aim of the country's independence. The government in Istanbul was under pressure from the Allied powers. This constitution was of a provisional character, since it was intended for the period of war and national resistance. // On 20 January 1921 the Grand National Assembly in Ankara voted the first constitution, which established national sovereignty as the basis of the state. The text belonged to the process of the war of liberation and rested on the principle that power belongs to the nation. The vote strengthened the legitimacy of the new authority. The Grand National Assembly gathered in Ankara, which thus became the centre of the new government. // The Constitution of 1921 formed the basis for the creation of the Turkish Republic, which was proclaimed in 1923. The idea of national sovereignty became a central element of the new political order. This experience remains a point of reference in the history of modern Turkey and of its relations with Europe. The principles of the text formed the basis for the later regime of the Republic founded in 1923.

analysis|01-20|1942|Η Διάσκεψη του Βάνζεε|The Wannsee Conference|In early 1942 Germany was at war on many fronts, and the Nazi regime had already begun the mass deportations and murders of Jews in Eastern Europe. The leaders of the Third Reich sought to coordinate the measures linked to the extermination of the Jews. This decision had already been taken at a higher level. The meeting lasted a few hours and was accompanied by minutes recorded in carefully bureaucratic language. // On 20 January 1942 senior officials met at the villa in Wannsee, near Berlin, and coordinated the "Final Solution", that is, the systematic extermination of the Jews of Europe. The meeting had the character of a formal conference, with discussion of the administrative aspects of the plan. Representatives of ministries and of the security services of the Nazi state took part in the conference. // The conference accelerated and organised the genocide, which led to the murder of about six million Jews. The event is one of the darkest chapters of European history. The memory of the Holocaust continues to teach about the dangers of racism and bureaucratic complicity. These minutes are today a key historical document on the coordination of the genocide. Understanding the context of the era helps in interpreting the decisions taken then.

analysis|01-20|1961|Ο Τζον Κένεντι ορκίζεται πρόεδρος|John F. Kennedy is sworn in as president|John F. Kennedy was elected in 1960 by a narrow margin over Richard Nixon, in elections that gave great importance to foreign policy. The Cold War had heightened the tension between the United States and the Soviet Union. The new president was young and promised a renewal of the country's political life. The swearing-in ceremony took place in cold weather and before a large crowd, with the speech broadcast live. // On 20 January 1961 Kennedy was sworn in as president, and in his speech he said the phrase "Ask not what your country can do for you". The text appealed to political responsibility and voluntary participation by citizens. The speech immediately became a symbol of the new spirit. Kennedy announced goals for the progress of space research, with the programme for a landing on the Moon. // His term included the Cuban missile crisis of 1962 and the promotion of civil rights. Kennedy was assassinated in 1963, and the administration passed to Lyndon Johnson. His speech remains one of the best-known texts in American political history. The succession by Lyndon Johnson brought changes in domestic politics and in legislation on civil rights.

analysis|01-20|2009|Ο Μπαράκ Ομπάμα ορκίζεται πρόεδρος|Barack Obama is sworn in as president|The election of Barack Obama in 2008 was a landmark for the United States, since he was the first African American to be elected to the office. The country was then facing the deep economic crisis of 2008, with bank failures and unemployment. His election campaign had been based on promises of change and unity. The swearing-in ceremony took place at the Capitol, with a very large crowd in Washington. // On 20 January 2009 Obama was sworn in as president, before a crowd of people in Washington. The ceremony had a historic character, as the development was regarded as pivotal for American society. His speech set goals for the economy, health and foreign policy. His first term began with measures to stabilise the economy and recover the banks. // His term included the reform of the health system, known as the Affordable Care Act, and the international climate agreement. His election opened discussions about racial equality and political representation. His story remains one of the most important chapters of contemporary American politics. This period remains a point of reference for debates about political representation in the United States. This historical development continues to be studied by researchers and historians around the world.

analysis|01-20|2025|Ο Ντόναλντ Τραμπ ορκίζεται 47ος πρόεδρος των ΗΠΑ|Donald Trump is sworn in as the 47th president of the US|Donald Trump had served as president of the United States from 2017 to 2021, before losing the 2020 election to Joe Biden. His return to office followed a new election campaign, with emphasis on immigration, the economy and foreign policy. The political division of the country remained intense. The ceremony took place inside the Capitol, and was accompanied by the presence of leaders and politicians from many countries. // On 20 January 2025 Trump was sworn in as the 47th president of the United States, returning to the White House four years after his previous term. The ceremony took place in Washington, in accordance with the constitutional procedure. His speech announced the basic priorities of the new administration. The first decisions of the new administration concerned immigration, trade and energy issues. // The new term is expected to bring changes in many areas of domestic and foreign policy. The effects of these decisions will be examined over time and will largely determine the relations of the United States with its allies. This period has already provoked wide public debate about the nature of presidential power. The development of these measures remains the subject of continuing discussion in the media and in Congress.

analysis|01-21|1793|Εκτελείται ο Λουδοβίκος ΙΣΤ΄|Louis XVI is executed|During the French Revolution the monarchy had already been greatly weakened. The king's attempted escape in 1791 had shaken the people's trust, and the National Assembly abolished the monarchy in 1792. Internal turmoil and war with the European powers intensified the political tension. The execution took place before a large crowd, in a square that is today called the Place de la Concorde. // Louis XVI was tried by the National Convention, accused of treason, and sentenced to death. On 21 January 1793 he was executed by guillotine in the Place de la Révolution in Paris. The execution provoked strong reaction in Europe and intensified the confrontation with the monarchies. The death sentence was passed by a narrow majority, which shows the divided public opinion. // The execution was one of the most symbolic events of the Revolution, and it was followed by the period of the Terror. France found itself at war with many European states, with internal conflicts and political assassinations. The history of the execution remains a central theme in the history of revolutions and of social change. The decision provoked reactions in the European states, which united in an alliance against France. The significance of the event can also be seen in the way societies remember it today.

analysis|01-21|1924|Πεθαίνει ο Λένιν|Lenin dies|Vladimir Lenin was the principal leader of the October Revolution of 1917 and of the creation of the Soviet Union. After the civil war he introduced the New Economic Policy, which allowed limited private initiative. His health had been shaken by a series of strokes in his last years. Lenin left behind a party that was already facing internal disagreements about the course of the country. // Lenin died on 21 January 1924, at the age of 53, on an estate near Moscow. His funeral was large, and the country faced a period of succession. The party leadership was now discussing the future of power. His funeral gathered a large crowd in Moscow, and his body was placed in a mausoleum in Red Square. // His death opened the way for Stalin, who gradually strengthened his position in the party and the state. This development led to a long period of authoritarian rule. Lenin remains one of the most controversial figures of the twentieth century. The discussions about succession led to confrontations, with Trotsky and Stalin at the centre. Understanding the context of the era helps in interpreting the decisions taken then.

analysis|01-21|1925|Η Αλβανία γίνεται δημοκρατία|Albania becomes a republic|After the First World War Albania faced political instability and foreign influences from neighbouring countries. Internal disputes between tribal leaders and political groups were intense. The need for stable government became pressing. The new system provided for an elected parliament and a president, based on the constitutional principles of the era. // On 21 January 1925 the Constituent Assembly proclaimed the country a republic, with Ahmet Zogu as its first president. The decision corresponded to a constitutional change and to the organisation of the state's institutions. Zogu already had a significant political role in the country. Zogu gradually assumed greater control of government, and the political parties were restricted. // This republic did not last long, as Zogu proclaimed himself king in 1928. The period of his regime was characterised by authoritarian measures and gradual dependence on foreign powers. This history shows the difficulties of the democratic institution in uncertain conditions. This situation left Albania vulnerable to the foreign influences that arrived at the end of the 1930s. The discussion on the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life. This historical development continues to be studied by researchers and historians around the world.

analysis|01-21|1976|Αρχίζουν οι εμπορικές πτήσεις του Κονκόρντ|Concorde begins commercial flights|Concorde was a supersonic passenger aircraft, developed by Britain and France in the 1960s. The project had a large technological cost, and its viability was questioned from the start. The prospect of travelling faster than sound made the aircraft a symbol of the era. Concorde had a speed close to twice the speed of sound, something unusual for a passenger aircraft. // On 21 January 1976 its commercial flights began, with services from London and Paris to distant destinations. Flight at supersonic speed allowed a significant reduction in travel time. Passengers were limited because of the high cost of tickets. The flights ran on set routes with limited capacity, which made the cost particularly high. // The aircraft operated for decades, until its withdrawal in 2003, after the accident of 2000. Its commercial success was limited, but its technological legacy remains important. Concorde is regarded today as a symbol of supersonic aviation and of the ambitions of the era. Its history remains instructive about the difficulties of cooperation between states in large technological investments. This historical development continues to be studied by researchers and historians around the world. The sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events.

analysis|01-22|1506|Οι πρώτοι Ελβετοί φρουροί φτάνουν στο Βατικανό|The first Swiss Guards arrive at the Vatican|In the early sixteenth century Pope Julius II sought reliable military protection for the Vatican and Rome. Swiss mercenaries were renowned for their reliability and discipline. Their choice reflected the military traditions of the era. The guards came from the Catholic cantons of Switzerland, and their selection was based on faith and reliability. // On 22 January 1506 one hundred and fifty Swiss men arrived at the Vatican and were taken on as the pope's guard. This group formed the core of today's Pontifical Swiss Guard. The arrival was accompanied by ceremonies and a demonstration of loyalty to the pope. During the sack of Rome in 1527, many of them were killed while protecting the pope. // This guard has been maintained to the present day, and its uniforms with their bright colours have become a symbol of the Vatican. Its presence is regarded as a historical tradition of the Church. The guard continues to carry out security and ceremonial duties. The tradition of the guard is today one of the best-known features of the Vatican and a tourist attraction. The sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events. The significance of the event can also be seen in the way societies remember it today.

analysis|01-22|1879|Η μάχη του Ισαντλγουάνα|The Battle of Isandlwana|At the end of 1878 the British Empire attempted to impose control over the Zulu kingdom of southern Africa, in a conflict known as the Zulu War. The British believed they could easily dominate, but they underestimated the military organisation of the Zulus. The invasion of their territory led to immediate confrontation. The British army had been divided into detachments, and the camp at Isandlwana had limited fortification. // On 22 January 1879 the Zulus attacked a British camp at Isandlwana and defeated the British forces with heavy losses. The battle was one of the most striking victories of indigenous armies against a European army. The British army suffered a great defeat in the area. More than a thousand British soldiers were killed in the battle, and many weapons and supplies were lost. // The defeat caused shock in Britain, and the expedition to Zululand was reinforced. In July 1879 the British defeated the Zulus at Ulundi, and the war came to an end. The battle remains an important point in the history of South Africa. This battle remains in history as one of the most significant military defeats of the British colonial era. The significance of the event can also be seen in the way societies remember it today.

analysis|01-22|1901|Πεθαίνει η Βασίλισσα Βικτώρια|Queen Victoria dies|Victoria ascended the British throne in 1837 and reigned for more than six decades. Her era was named Victorian and was characterised by industrial development, imperial expansion and social change. The queen played an important role as a symbol of national identity. Her reign was linked with the Industrial Revolution, colonial expansion and the broadening of education. // Victoria died on 22 January 1901 at Osborne House, on the Isle of Wight, at the age of 81. Her death shook the country and the empire. Her son Edward ascended the throne as Edward VII. The queen gained great popularity and had a strong personal influence within her family and in international diplomacy. // The era of her reign left a strong legacy in British culture, architecture and institutional life. Her influence is still felt in modern Britain and in its former colonies. The queen remains a reference point for the era that took her name. Her funeral was a great ceremony, with the presence of leaders from many countries and crowds of citizens. Understanding the context of the era helps in interpreting the decisions taken then. The discussion on the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life.

analysis|01-22|1973|Η απόφαση Ρόου κατά Γουέιντ|Roe v. Wade ruling|In the United States of the 1970s, state laws on abortion differed and were often strict. The case reached the Supreme Court, invoking the constitutional protection of privacy. The issue provoked intense political and religious disputes. The decision was based on earlier rulings on privacy, which concerned matters of family life. // On 22 January 1973 the Supreme Court decided that the constitutional right to privacy covers the decision on abortion, at defined stages of pregnancy. The decision correspondingly limited the legislative regulation of the states. The vote was divided, with significant disagreements among the justices. Its impact on American society was enormous, with continuing legal and political battles in the states. // This decision was a central point of American legal and political life for almost fifty years. It was overturned in 2022 by the Dobbs decision, which returned the issue to the states. The case is still associated with intense social and political debate. Its reversal in 2022 led to new legislative arrangements in many states and to continuing discussion. The discussion on the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life. This historical development continues to be studied by researchers and historians around the world.

analysis|01-23|1849|Η πρώτη γυναίκα γιατρός στις ΗΠΑ|The first woman doctor in the US|In the nineteenth century women in the United States faced serious obstacles in gaining access to medical education, and most medical schools did not admit them. Medicine was regarded as a male profession, and many questioned women's ability. The need for women doctors was nonetheless evident, particularly for women patients. Her admission to medical school was the result of persistent efforts and the support of some professors. // Elizabeth Blackwell was admitted to a medical school in Geneva, New York, and graduated in 1849 with a medical degree. She was the first woman to receive such a degree in the United States. Her success was difficult, since she met intense suspicion. She herself later taught and strengthened the education of women in medicine, through institutions and initiatives. // Blackwell later founded a hospital for women and children in New York, and helped to create a medical school for women. Her path opened the way for many women doctors. Her story is today regarded as an important milestone for women's access to science. Her personal path is today regarded as a model for women who pursue careers in traditionally male fields. This historical development continues to be studied by researchers and historians around the world.

analysis|01-23|1957|Το «φρίσμπι» αποκτά όνομα|The Frisbee gets its name|In the early 1950s students at Yale often threw the empty metal pie tins of the Frisbie Pie Company, which operated in the area. Playing with the pie tins was popular among young people and spread across university campuses. The idea of a flying disc for entertainment was already in the air. This object thus became an occasion for play outdoors. The game spread very quickly in the United States and then in many countries, with different local versions and rules. // Walter Morrison, a painter and engineer, made a plastic disc that resembled the students' pie tins, and in 1957 sold the design to the Wham-O company. The company named it the Frisbee, based on the name of the Frisbie pie company. The product went on sale quickly and sold millions of units. The name thus became the common name of the game. The commercial success of the product rested on cheap manufacture and easy transport. // The Frisbee developed into a sporting activity with its own rules, and later into a sport known as Ultimate. Games of it in parks and on beaches bring together people of all ages. The tradition of the Frisbee is today linked with modern outdoor entertainment. Its history shows how a simple habit of students can become a worldwide phenomenon. Today disc games are linked with sporting events and community activities around the world.

analysis|01-23|1960|Το Trieste κατεβαίνει στο βαθύτερο σημείο των ωκεανών|Trieste descends to the deepest point of the oceans|Exploring the great depths of the oceans was for decades difficult, because the pressures at depth are enormous. Auguste Piccard developed the bathyscaphe, a kind of submarine with float tanks, which allowed controlled descent. The first experiments of this type had been carried out in the Mediterranean and the Adriatic. The idea was for humans to reach the deepest region of the planet. The descent was the result of many years of technical testing and development, which included checking the strength of materials under pressure. // On 23 January 1960 the bathyscaphe Trieste, carrying Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, descended into the Mariana Trench in the Pacific, to a depth of almost eleven kilometres. The descent lasted hours, with a small observation window and limited communication. The success was unique, since no human had ever reached that point before. The crew had limited time at depth and followed strict safety procedures. // The record of the Trieste stood for decades, until the dives of 2012 with modern submersibles. The mission paved the way for research into the deep oceans and for understanding life in extreme conditions. Scientists continue today to study the deep ecosystems discovered in these regions. The descent remains one of the most important achievements of oceanography. This achievement was widely recognised by the scientific community and the media of the era.

analysis|01-24|41|Ο Κλαύδιος γίνεται αυτοκράτορας|Claudius becomes emperor|In the first century AD the Roman Empire rested on the family of Augustus and on the court at Rome, where rivalries were frequent. Gaius, known as Caligula, had ruled with authoritarianism and eccentricities that provoked the reaction of the Senate and the officers. The situation was unstable, with conspiracies and fear. Claudius, his uncle, was not regarded as the most likely successor. Claudius strengthened the imperial administration with new officials, and among them were freedmen in the bureaucracy. // According to the sources, Caligula was assassinated in early AD 41, and afterwards the Praetorian Guard proclaimed Claudius emperor. The proclamation was unusual, since the state had not yet established a mechanism of succession. The Senate was forced to accept the choice, despite its initial reactions. This administrative change affected the functioning of the empire for several years. // The reign of Claudius, which lasted until AD 54, included administrative reforms and the British campaign of AD 43. The emperor strengthened the bureaucracy of the empire and extended the rights of certain provinces. His era left a form of power that the following emperors also followed. Historians today examine the sources on his life with care. The period of his reign is also known from public building works in Rome.

analysis|01-24|1848|Βρίσκεται χρυσός στην Καλιφόρνια|Gold is found in California|In the mid-nineteenth century California was sparsely populated and belonged to Mexico until 1848. The area of New Helvetia, which belonged to John Sutter, attracted migrants and workers for agricultural jobs. The need for timber was great, so sawmills operated on the rivers. The landscape was already known to few people. News of the gold attracted people from many places, many of whom travelled far by ship to reach the area. // In January 1848 James Marshall, a worker building a sawmill on the river of the area, saw pieces of gold in the water of the channel. The news spread at first slowly, since Sutter tried to keep it secret. Soon, however, the rumour reached the urban centres of the coast. The lack of organised infrastructure created difficulties for the living conditions and the safety of the workers. // The "gold rush" attracted hundreds of thousands of people from the United States and abroad. San Francisco grew quickly, and California became a state in 1850. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which had been signed shortly before, had already incorporated the area into the United States. The event permanently changed the demography and economy of the west coast. The rapid growth of the population soon changed the image of the region.

analysis|01-24|1965|Πεθαίνει ο Ουίνστον Τσόρτσιλ|Winston Churchill dies|Winston Churchill had led Britain through the Second World War as prime minister, and his leadership in the difficult months of 1940 has remained in history. His literary and political activity was very wide. In the last years of his life he had withdrawn from active politics. His health was already weak. Churchill had been re-elected prime minister in 1951 and had been called on to manage the problems of post-war Britain. // Churchill died on 24 January 1965 in London, at the age of 90. His funeral was held with state honours, and it was the first time in more than a century that such honours had been given to a non-royal figure. Thousands of people stood in the streets to bid him farewell. His work was recognised with the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953, for his writing. // This funeral was one of the largest ceremonies in British history, with the participation of leaders from many countries. His memory remains strong as a symbol of resistance to the Nazi threat. His political path and his writings continue to be studied by historians and analysts. His presence is regarded as central to the British history of the twentieth century. His funeral was a major public ceremony with international participation.

analysis|01-24|1972|Βρίσκεται Ιάπωνας στρατιώτης στη ζούγκλα του Γκουάμ|Japanese soldier found in the jungle of Guam|Shoichi Yokoi was a sergeant of the Japanese army who served on Guam during the Second World War. After the American occupation of the island, several Japanese soldiers refused to surrender and continued to hide in the jungle. Their notions of honour and discipline were deeply rooted. Life in the jungle was hard and isolated. Yokoi lived in a simple shelter and made his tools from jungle materials, keeping up his military habits. // On 24 January 1972 Yokoi was found by hunters near a river on Guam, after 28 years in isolation. He himself lived in a shelter and fed on whatever he could find. The discovery moved Japan, which welcomed him as a national symbol of discipline. His discovery took place near the river, when two people spotted his traces. // Yokoi returned to Japan and became the object of great public interest. His story showed how long the consequences of the war could last in an individual life. Yokoi died later, and his story remains a case study in the psychology of isolation. His case is one of the most unusual chapters of the Pacific War. His story received wide coverage in the Japanese and international press.

analysis|01-25|1919|Αποφασίζεται η Κοινωνία των Εθνών|The League of Nations is decided|After the First World War, Wilson and other leaders believed that an international organisation was needed to prevent new conflicts. The idea had already been set out in the Fourteen Points and in earlier discussions of international cooperation. The negotiation over the form of the organisation was difficult. The disputes concerned mainly the power of the members and the guarantees. The Covenant formed part of the peace treaty, and the member states committed themselves to respect borders. // At the Paris Peace Conference, on 25 January 1919, the commission approved the statute of the organisation, known as the Covenant of the League of Nations. The text provided for collective security, arbitration and the possibility of sanctions. Its incorporation into the peace treaties gave the organisation a legal basis. The League of Nations began to operate in Geneva the following year. The organisation had bodies such as the Council and the Assembly, with meetings in Geneva. // The League of Nations dealt with many international issues, with some successes in arbitration and humanitarian matters. However, the lack of strong enforcement mechanisms and the absence of the United States weakened its functioning. The organisation was replaced by the United Nations after the Second World War. Its experience provided an important lesson for international cooperation. The idea of an international organisation thus remains central to modern diplomacy. The composition of the Council included permanent members from the great powers.

analysis|01-25|1924|Αρχίζουν οι πρώτοι Χειμερινοί Ολυμπιακοί Αγώνες|The first Winter Olympic Games begin|In the early twentieth century the Olympic Games were mainly summer events, and winter sports had limited recognition. The International Olympic Committee decided to organise a special event for winter sports. The mountain areas of the Alps were ideal for skiing and ice competitions. The idea had been discussed for several years. The athletes of the event were mainly Europeans and Americans, with smaller participation from other countries. // On 25 January 1924 the competitions began at Chamonix in France, with athletes from sixteen countries. The events included skiing, skating and other winter activities. The event was simple but successful, with large public participation. The skiing and ice sports had already had a tradition in the northern regions of Europe. // The Chamonix Games are regarded as the start of the modern winter event, and 1924 became a recognised year for the Winter Olympics. Four years later the games were repeated at St. Moritz in Switzerland and were established as a regular event. Today the Winter Olympic Games are held every four years, with extensive television coverage. Their beginning at Chamonix remains a point of reference for the history of sport. Later editions expanded to more sports and to new countries.

analysis|01-25|1945|Τελειώνει η μάχη των Αρδεννών|The Battle of the Bulge ends|At the end of 1944 Germany launched a surprise counter-offensive on the Western Front, in the wooded area of the Ardennes. The aim was to split the Allied forces and to reach the port of Antwerp. The attack caught the Allies by surprise, and the front formed a bulge, known as the "bulge". The battles were fierce, with snow and bad weather. The American soldiers of the area suffered heavy losses, but continued the resistance at the critical points. // With the improvement of the weather, Allied air bombing proved effective, and the German reserves were exhausted. The German army gradually withdrew, and in January 1945 the Allies restored their positions. The battle officially ended on 25 January, and the German operation had failed. Bastogne, a road junction in the area, held out for several days under siege. // This defeat weakened the German forces, which were unable to regain the initiative on the Western Front. Losses were heavy on both sides, with thousands killed and wounded. The development hastened the Allied advance into Germany. The Battle of the Bulge remains one of the best-known episodes of the Second World War. This resistance paved the way for the final Allied advance.

analysis|01-25|2011|Αρχίζει η εξέγερση στην Αίγυπτο|The uprising begins in Egypt|In the early twenty-first century Egypt was governed by Hosni Mubarak, who had been in power for almost three decades. Unemployment, corruption and police repression caused intense dissatisfaction, particularly among young people. Social conditions were difficult, with low wages and limited opportunities. Uprisings in Tunisia had already shown that change was possible.
